title: Gauhati High Court Says PAN, Voter ID Alone Cannot Prove Citizenship
excerpt: In Kulchan Begum's case, the court held that PAN cards and EPICs issued on self-application are not proof of citizenship unless the records behind them are proved, and upheld a Foreigners Tribunal opinion.
body:
• The Gauhati High Court held on November 5, 2026 that a PAN card and a voter ID (EPIC) alone cannot prove Indian citizenship, because both are issued on self-application without formal enquiry.
  • The ruling, in Kulchan Begum v. Union of India & Ors., upheld a Foreigners Tribunal opinion declaring the petitioner a foreigner of the post-March 25, 1971 stream and dismissed her writ petition.
  • Anyone facing a citizenship case in Assam still has to prove the records behind such documents, plus family linkage and, under Section 6A(2), continuous residence — the documents alone will not discharge the burden under Section 9 of the Foreigners Act, 1946.
  • The court recalled the petitioner's interim bail granted on April 18, 2022 and said the consequences of the tribunal's opinion would follow.

A PAN card and a voter identity card, on their own, are not proof of Indian citizenship, the Gauhati High Court has held, because both documents are issued on self-application without any formal enquiry by the issuing authority.

A Division Bench of Justice Kalyan Rai Surana and Justice Susmita Phukan Khaund pronounced the judgment on November 5, 2026, dismissing a writ petition by Kulchan Begum of Darrang district, whom a Foreigners Tribunal had declared a foreigner of the post-March 25, 1971 stream, according to reports by LawChakra and CourtBook.

What the court actually said

The bench's reasoning turns on how the two documents are made, not on what they show. In the passage quoted by both reports, the court said:

"The PAN Card and EPIC exhibited by the petitioner… is not a proof of citizenship. These are documents that are issued on self-application without any formal enquiry by the Income Tax Department and Election Commission of India. Therefore, unless, the records supplementing the PAN Card and EPIC are proved, the said exhibited documents cannot be accepted as a proof of citizenship of India."

That is a before-and-after point worth stating precisely. The judgment does not cancel anyone's PAN card or voter ID, and it does not change who may vote or pay tax. What it settles, for citizenship proceedings, is the evidentiary weight of those documents: they identify a person, but they do not, without the underlying records being proved, establish that the person is a citizen.

Who is affected, exactly

The ruling directly governs people whose citizenship is being tested before a Foreigners Tribunal in Assam — the class of cases where, under Section 9 of the Foreigners Act, 1946, the burden of proving citizenship lies on the person whose status is questioned. It is not a general change to electoral rolls or tax records.

In this case, the petitioner said she was born on April 25, 1977 in Assam and relied on voter lists from 1966 and 1970 said to contain her projected grandparents' names, her projected father's PAN card, voter ID and election records, and her own PAN card, EPIC, ration card and an NRC application acknowledgement.

The court found that material insufficient on two separate grounds. First, the documents did not prove her linkage to her projected father: the municipal certificate was not proved through its author, the NRC acknowledgement was not supported by the original, and the ration card and 2018 voter list did not establish the relationship. Second, under Section 6A(2) of the Citizenship Act, 1955, she had to show continuous residence in Assam of her grandparents and father, and there was no evidence for the period between 1970 and 1997.

The court also held that her projected father's candidature in Lok Sabha and Assembly elections and his service as a Guwahati Municipal Corporation councillor did not by themselves prove that she was his daughter.

How the case reached the High Court

The Foreigners Tribunal (4th), Mangaldai, gave its opinion on August 21, 2018. The petitioner argued before the High Court that her earlier lawyer had wrongly advised her not to examine her parents and others, and that she had not been heard. The bench rejected both pleas on the tribunal's own record: she had been given several adjournments to examine other witnesses and did not do so, the wrong-advice plea was called an after-thought, and the record showed her counsel was heard on July 20, 2018 before the opinion. The plea of no hearing was described as ex facie false.

What to do next, if you face a similar case

On the court's own logic, the practical step is evidentiary, not rhetorical: keep and be ready to prove the records that sit behind a PAN card or EPIC, and be ready to prove family linkage and residence through primary evidence or witnesses, rather than relying on the cards alone. The judgment shows a writ court will not reopen a tribunal finding to allow a fresh round of evidence on a plea of poor legal advice that the record does not support.

The writ petition, WP(C) No. 2459 of 2020, was dismissed with no order as to costs. The court recalled and revoked the interim bail granted on April 18, 2022, and directed that the consequences of the Foreigners Tribunal's opinion would follow.
